title: Colorado judge finds ICE in contempt for instant re-arrests borrowed from Minnesota agents

 Crime, Law and Justice Cait Kelley November 18, 2026 4:29 PM Colorado judge finds ICE in contempt for instant re-arrests borrowed from Minnesota agents
 The Whipple Federal Building pictured in May. It's been the site of multiple instant ICE re-arrests of immigrants ordered released by federal judges. Kerem Yücel | MPR News Go Deeper.

 ICE instantly re-arrested at least 18 people in Colorado before an official promised under oath to stop. A federal judge held the government in contempt but won’t take further action because the re-arrests have ceased. A Colorado federal judge held an immigration official and the government in contempt Wednesday for instantly re-arresting a man she had ordered released. However, the judge declined to take further action because an official swore in court the agency had ended the practice in Colorado.
 In two hearings, Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials tried to justify the re-arrest to U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney. Acting Denver Field Office Director Nathan Rasper said he had ordered instant re-arrests of some immigrants released by judges after hearing from “colleagues” in Minnesota that courts had allowed it.
 In Wednesday’s order, Sweeney held Nichole Black, ICE’s assistant field office director in Denver, and the government in contempt for the re-arrest.
 “This should — and, in the Court’s opinion, must — shock any reader. There is not a single word in this Nation’s Constitution that sustains or could plausibly give rise to Ms. Black’s ‘belief’ that ICE and ICE agents can walk out to the sidewalk and re-shackle a habeas petitioner within a minute of that petitioner’s court-ordered release,” Sweeney wrote.

 ♡ Donate now Sweeney added that “the single thing” that saves Black and the government from further action by the court in this case is Rasper’s testimony that ICE had “ceased” these re-arrests as a result of the first evidentiary hearing Nov. 4. Sweeney wrote that “cured” the contempt, but reminded the government she considers Rasper’s pledge legally binding.
 In a statement to MPR News last week, an unnamed ICE spokesperson wrote: “When appropriate, ICE will address the issues identified by the court and take further action consistent with applicable law and court orders, which can include rearresting an offender.”
 At least one other federal judge in Colorado has ruled against an instant ICE re-arrest. In a Nov. 3 order , U.S. District Judge S. Kato Crews said ICE never really released a man it instantly re-arrested and wrote: "Once again, the cruelty appears to be the point."
 Crews cited decisions from two Minnesota judges who ruled similar re-arrests violated their release orders.
 Minnesota’s district court is split on the issue: while two judges have strongly condemned the re-arrests, two others have ruled the re-arrests did not violate their release orders.
 MPR News has confirmed at least eight men have been instantly re-arrested at the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building after they were ordered released by a judge. One man was re-arrested twice.
 Elizabeth Jordan, a law professor at the University of Denver, teamed up with the ACLU of Colorado on an amicus brief asking Sweeney to take ‘necessary steps’ to stop the re-arrests.
 The brief called the re-arrests “part of a pattern in this District and nationally of ICE’s circumvention and violation of federal court orders.”
 For now, it appears the re-arrests have stopped in Colorado. 
 Court records show ICE instantly re-arrested at least 18 people between Oct. 27 and Nov. 4, sometimes in batches. Those people have since been re-released.
 But Jordan said damage has been done to the immigrants, their families and the rule of law.
 “All of these people who thought they were going to be released and put their confidence in the word of a federal judge probably felt betrayed,” she said. 
 “U.S. citizen children were taught the lesson by ICE that a court order doesn’t mean something,” Jordan added.
